title: The Urban Watershed Mystery
subtitle: Environmental Science Investigation
summary: Fish populations in Riverdale Creek dropped sharply after spring storms. Investigate the runoff sources, analyze water chemistry data, choose your next lead, brief the City Council, and write an evidence-based remediation plan.

briefing.scene: After two days of heavy spring storms, dead fish have washed up along three miles of Riverdale Creek. The Riverdale Water Authority has handed you a field kit, four test stations, and a deadline: the City Council meets on Thursday night.
briefing.goal: Work out what caused the oxygen crash, choose which lead to follow, brief the council out loud, and write a recommendation that fixes the cause, not just the symptom.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vance
turns.text: This is Dr. Vance with the Riverdale Water Authority. Yesterday's storm dropped 2.4 inches of rain in six hours, and this morning we had reports of dead fish along three miles of Riverdale Creek.

turns.speaker: Tomás Reyes
turns.text: I'm at Station 1, upstream in the forest preserve. Dissolved oxygen is 8 parts per million, the water is 14 degrees Celsius, and I can see live trout in the pools.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vance
turns.text: Good. Healthy streams stay above 5 parts per million, so Station 1 is fine. What about the stations downstream?

turns.speaker: Tomás Reyes
turns.text: At Station 2, below the industrial park, oxygen plunged to 2 parts per million, and there is a thin foam on the surface. At Station 3, beside the community park, oxygen is 6 parts per million, but the water is the color of chocolate milk because of heavy sediment.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vance
turns.text: So the sediment is worst at Station 3, but the oxygen emergency is at Station 2. Your team must decide whether fertilizer runoff, industrial waste, or soil erosion is the main cause. The City Council meets on Thursday, and they need an answer.

report.title: Riverdale Watershed Runoff Report
text: Urban runoff happens when rain flows over impervious surfaces, such as asphalt, roofs, and packed soil, instead of soaking into the ground. Fast-moving runoff carries fertilizer, oil, soil, and trash straight into creeks with almost no natural filtering.

Lawn fertilizer is rich in nitrates, which feed algae. After a storm, the algae can multiply into a thick bloom. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen in the water, creating a hypoxic zone: an area with too little oxygen for fish to breathe. Water-quality guidelines warn that oxygen below 4 parts per million stresses fish, and near 2 parts per million most species cannot survive.

Chemical tests at Station 2 found high nitrate levels together with surfactants and phosphates, which come from soap and detergents such as the wash water at commercial car washes. Phosphates feed algae just as nitrates do. Sediment, by contrast, mostly makes water cloudy; it blocks sunlight but does not by itself use up oxygen. Engineers therefore suspect that lawns and a car wash drain, not soil erosion, caused the oxygen crash.

drain.title: Interview: Car Wash Drain Inspection
drain.summary: A car wash next to Station 2 sends soapy wash water, with surfactants and phosphates, into a storm drain that flows to Riverdale Creek 40 meters above Station 2.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: I traced the pipe behind the Eastside Car Wash. It does not connect to the sewage plant. It empties into a storm drain that runs straight to Riverdale Creek, forty meters above Station 2.

turns.speaker: Mr. Okafor
turns.text: We wash about three hundred cars a day, and the soapy water goes down that drain. Nobody ever told us it ends up in the creek.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Water from the drain tested at 38 milligrams per liter of surfactants and 4.1 milligrams per liter of phosphate. A healthy stream carries almost none of either.

survey.title: Maple Heights Lawn Fertilizer Survey
survey.summary: A survey of 100 homes in the Maple Heights neighborhood above Station 2 found that 66 had fertilized their lawns in the two weeks before the storm.

slope.summary: A bare slope at the community park lost 48 kilograms of soil per 100 square meters, eight times as much as grass. Erosion is real, but it explains the cloudy water at Station 3 more than the low oxygen at Station 2.

phases.title: Field Dispatch from Dr. Vance
phases.instructions: Listen to the dispatch. Pay attention to the oxygen reading at each station and to Dr. Vance's number for a healthy stream. Then answer two questions and pin the best evidence to your board.

tasks.q: Why is Station 2 the biggest emergency on Dr. Vance's list?

options.text: The water there looked brown because of heavy sediment.
It was the only station where live fish were seen.
Its dissolved oxygen dropped to 2 parts per million.
Its oxygen reading was lower than the reading at Station 1.

tasks.explain: Tomás reports that at Station 2 "oxygen plunged to 2 parts per million," and Dr. Vance says healthy streams stay above 5. The brown, sediment-heavy water was at Station 3, and live trout were seen at Station 1.

tasks.q: Which conclusion do the station readings best support?

options.text: The oxygen problem began somewhere between Station 1 and Station 2.
The storm made the whole creek equally unhealthy.
Heavy sediment at Station 3 is the main reason the fish died downstream.
Station 1 had the lowest oxygen reading in the creek.

tasks.explain: Station 1 had 8 parts per million, but just downstream "at Station 2, below the industrial park, oxygen plunged to 2 parts per million." The change happened between the two stations, and Station 3 stayed at 6.

tasks.q: Choose the statements that support this claim: "Fish are in danger downstream of the industrial park."

pool.text: oxygen plunged to 2 parts per million
Yesterday's storm dropped 2.4 inches of rain in six hours
Healthy streams stay above 5 parts per million
the water is the color of chocolate milk because of heavy sediment
reports of dead fish along three miles of Riverdale Creek

phases.title: Dossier: Runoff Report and Station Data
phases.instructions: Read the report, then compare the oxygen chart with the water test log. Look for a pattern that connects two sources.

tasks.q: According to the report, how can lawn fertilizer lead to a low-oxygen zone in a creek?

options.text: Nitrates make the water too warm for fish to breathe.
Nitrates feed algae, and bacteria that decompose the dead algae use up the oxygen.
Nitrates cause algae to grow into a thick bloom that covers the surface of the creek.
Runoff moves quickly across asphalt, roofs, and packed soil.

tasks.explain: The report says nitrates "feed algae," and "when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen in the water." The bloom is only the first step, and the fast runoff explains how fertilizer reaches the creek, not how oxygen is lost.

tasks.q: In the report, what does "impervious" mean in the phrase "impervious surfaces"?

options.text: full of tiny holes that hold water
naturally warm and dry
polluted with oil and trash
not letting water soak through

tasks.explain: The report explains that rain flows over impervious surfaces "instead of soaking into the ground." Asphalt and roofs block water, so they do not let it soak through. Oil and trash are things runoff carries, not the meaning of the word.

tasks.q: Why is the heavy sediment at Station 3 probably NOT the main cause of the oxygen crash?

options.text: Cloudy water does not by itself use up oxygen, and Station 3 still had 6.0 ppm.
The report says soil never travels in runoff, so sediment cannot reach a creek at all.
Fish can survive in any water that is cloudy, so sediment is never harmful.
Station 3 is too far from the storm drains to be affected by runoff at all.

tasks.explain: The report says sediment "blocks sunlight but does not by itself use up oxygen," and the chart shows Station 3 at 6.0 ppm, well above the 4 ppm stress line. The report also says runoff does carry soil, so the first distractor reverses it.

tasks.q: Which conclusion is supported when you combine the oxygen chart and the water test log?

options.text: Where turbidity is highest, oxygen is lowest.
High nitrate readings appear only at Station 2.
The two lowest oxygen readings came at the two stations with the highest nitrates.
Oxygen at Station 4 (3.5 ppm) is higher than at Station 2 (2.0 ppm), so the creek recovers downstream.

tasks.explain: The chart shows the lowest oxygen at Station 2 (2.0) and Station 4 (3.5). The log shows the highest nitrates at those same stations (9.6 and 6.8 mg/L). Station 3 has the highest turbidity (140 NTU) but still 6.0 ppm oxygen.

tasks.q: A neighbor says, "Soil erosion from the community park killed the fish." Which evidence from the report and data most weakens her claim?

options.text: Station 3, beside the community park, had the heaviest sediment of all four stations, at 140 NTU.
Station 3 kept 6.0 ppm of oxygen, while the lowest oxygen came where nitrates were highest.
The report says runoff can carry soil, oil, and trash into creeks.
Station 3 is the only station with a bare, eroding slope nearby.

tasks.explain: A claim about erosion would predict the lowest oxygen at the most sediment. Instead Station 3 (turbidity 140 NTU) had 6.0 ppm, while Station 2 had 2.0 ppm with 9.6 mg/L of nitrate. The other options either support her claim or only repeat a background fact.

tasks.q: Choose the sentences from the report that support this claim: "Nutrient pollution, not sediment, is the most likely cause of the oxygen crash."

phases.title: Choose Your Next Lead
phases.instructions: You have time for only one field investigation before Thursday. Your choice unlocks new evidence for your board. The other leads are summarized for you, so the briefing and the recommendation work whichever lead you follow.

decision.q: The council meets Thursday and you have time for one field investigation. Which lead do you follow first?

options.text: Trace the pipe behind the car wash next to Station 2
options.consequence: The drain empties soapy wash water into a storm sewer 40 meters above Station 2. It tested high for surfactants and phosphate, and phosphate feeds algae the way fertilizer does. You have found one confirmed source.

board.label: Source lead
board.text: The Eastside Car Wash drain flows to the creek 40 meters above Station 2 and tested at 4.1 mg/L of phosphate.

options.text: Survey the lawns in the Maple Heights neighborhood
options.consequence: Sixty-six of 100 homes fertilized just before the storm, mostly on Maple Avenue and Oak Lane. You now have a second, much larger source of nitrates.

board.label: Source lead
board.text: 66 of 100 homes above Station 2 fertilized their lawns in the 14 days before the storm.

options.text: Measure soil loss on the bare slope at the community park
options.consequence: The bare slope lost 48 kg of soil per 100 square meters, so erosion is real. But it explains the cloudy water at Station 3, not the oxygen crash at Station 2. You will still need the data on nutrient sources.

board.label: Source lead
board.text: A bare slope lost 48 kg of soil per 100 square meters, but Station 3 still had 6.0 ppm of oxygen.

phases.title: Oral Briefing: City Council Emergency Session
phases.instructions: Plan your briefing with the four planner slots, then record 45 to 90 seconds. Use the numbers and evidence on your board.

task.title: Brief the City Council
task.scenario: It is Thursday night and the Riverdale City Council has packed the room. They want to know why the fish died. You are the junior hydrologist, and your evidence board is open.
task.prompt: Explain to the council what caused the oxygen crash at Station 2. Use at least two numbers from the data, describe how the pollution traveled from land to creek, and tell the council which source to fix first.

frames: The main cause of the fish kill was ___.
At Station 2, dissolved oxygen fell to ___, but at Station 1 it was ___.
This happened because ___ fed the algae, and then ___.
I recommend that the city fix ___ first because ___.
guided.model: Members of the council, the main cause of the fish kill was nutrient runoff. At Station 2, dissolved oxygen fell to 2.0 parts per million, but at Station 1 it was 8.0. This happened because nitrates from lawns and a car wash drain fed the algae, and then bacteria used up the oxygen when the algae died. I recommend that the city fix the storm drain first because it sends pollution straight to the creek.

successCriteria: I state one clear cause in my first sentence.
I use at least two numbers from the chart or log and compare them.
I explain the chain of events with a connecting word such as because or as a result.
I recommend one action and give a reason.

listenFor: A claim that names nutrient runoff rather than only 'pollution'
Comparison of Station 1 and Station 2 oxygen readings
Cause-and-effect connectors (because, as a result, which caused)
teacher.followUp: If sediment is also a problem, why is it not the first thing to fix?

phases.title: Remediation Plan and Recommendation
phases.instructions: Write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph for the council packet. Choose a fix that matches the cause you proved.

task.title: Write the Council Recommendation
task.scenario: The council will vote on a clean-up budget next week. Your written recommendation goes into their packet, and members will read it alongside the engineer's notes.
task.prompt: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that tells the council what caused the oxygen crash and what they should build or change. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the sources.

frames: The oxygen crash in Riverdale Creek was caused by ___.
For example, dissolved oxygen was ___ at Station 2, while nitrates reached ___.
This proves the cause because ___ feed algae, and when the algae die, ___.
guided.model: The oxygen crash in Riverdale Creek was caused by nutrient runoff, not by soil erosion. For example, dissolved oxygen was only 2.0 ppm at Station 2, while nitrates reached 9.6 mg/L. This proves the cause because nitrates feed algae, and when the algae die, bacteria use up the oxygen that fish need. Station 3 had the most sediment but still kept 6.0 ppm. Therefore, the council should build bioswales along Maple Avenue because they filter nitrates and soap before the water reaches the creek.

revisionPrompts.prompt: Add one more number from the chart or log. Which station does it come from?
Explain why Station 3's sediment does not prove your claim wrong.
Connect your evidence to your recommendation with a word such as therefore or as a result.

successCriteria: My claim names the cause in one sentence.
I cite at least two numbers and say which station they come from.
My reasoning explains how nitrates lead to low oxygen.
My recommendation is specific and matches my claim.

lookFor: A claim that names nutrient runoff
A reasoning sentence that explains the algae-to-oxygen chain
commonIssues: Listing numbers without explaining what they show
Naming sediment as the cause because it is the most visible
A recommendation that does not connect to the claim

teacherQuestions: Which two pieces of evidence best show that sediment was not the main cause? Which source did each one come from?
How did the lead you chose in the Decision phase change what was on your board? What would the other two leads have shown?
Explain the chain from a lawn to a dead fish using the words nitrate, algae, and dissolved oxygen.
What is the difference between treating a symptom, such as adding oxygen to the creek, and fixing the cause, such as reducing nutrient runoff?
debrief.connections: Connects to ecosystems, the water cycle, and human impact in science, and to civic decision-making in social studies. The same claim-evidence-reasoning pattern appears in the Newsroom and Space Colony missions.
